comments.comment: I think we're trowing too much math and then going to the conclusions. Let's provide the insights, interpretation as we write down the math. For example, Eq. 16 (diagnostic) may be introduced only at the end, connecting a theoretical argument with a quantifiable metric.

The key interpretation is that \\(\rho_t\\) measures gradient alignment, while \\(\kappa_t\\) measures curvature along the gradient direction. Their relationship describes how curvature rotates the gradient after an optimization step.Starting from\\[ \boxed{ \rho_t\approx\frac{\\|g\_{t-1}\\|}{\\|g_t\\|}(1-\eta\kappa_t) } \\]where\\[ \kappa_t= \frac{g\_{t-1}^{\top}H\_{t-1}g\_{t-1}} {\\|g\_{t-1}\\|^2} \\]is the Hessian curvature projected onto the gradient direction.## 1. Relationship between \\(\rho_t\\) and \\(\kappa_t\\)Assuming \\(\eta>0\\) and nonzero gradients:| Condition            | Gradient alignment   | Interpretation                                          || -------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- || \\(\eta\kappa_t<1\\) | \\(\rho_t>0\\)       | Gradients have a positive projection onto each other    || \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\) | \\(\rho_t\approx0\\) | Consecutive gradients are orthogonal                    || \\(\eta\kappa_t>1\\) | \\(\rho_t<0\\)       | Gradient direction reverses along the previous gradient |Thus, increasing positive curvature relative to the learning rate pushes gradient alignment from positive toward negative, although the exact magnitude of \\(\rho_t\\) also depends on the gradient norm ratio.## 2. What does \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\) mean geometrically?Consider the gradient descent update:\\[ \theta_t=\theta\_{t-1}-\eta g\_{t-1}. \\]Using a first-order approximation of the new gradient,\\[ g_t\approx g\_{t-1}-\eta H\_{t-1}g\_{t-1}. \\]Taking the inner product with the previous gradient,\\[ g\_{t-1}^{\top}g_t \approx \\|g\_{t-1}\\|^2(1-\eta\kappa_t). \\]Therefore, when\\[ \boxed{\eta\kappa_t=1} \\]we obtain\\[ \boxed{g\_{t-1}^{\top}g_t\approx0.} \\]Geometrically, the updated gradient has lost its component along the previous gradient direction. If the updated gradient remains nonzero, the two gradients are approximately orthogonal.## 3. Connection to the optimal learning rateThere is an important interpretation here.Consider a second-order Taylor approximation of the loss along the negative gradient direction:\\[ \mathcal L(\theta\_{t-1}-\eta g\_{t-1}) \approx \mathcal L(\theta\_{t-1}) -\eta\\|g\_{t-1}\\|^2 +\frac{\eta^2}{2}\kappa_t\\|g\_{t-1}\\|^2. \\]Differentiating with respect to \\(\eta\\):\\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\eta} \approx -\\|g\_{t-1}\\|^2(1-\eta\kappa_t). \\]Setting this derivative to zero gives\\[ \boxed{\eta^\*=\frac{1}{\kappa_t}} \\]for \\(\kappa_t>0\\).So \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\) corresponds to the locally optimal step size along the negative gradient direction under the quadratic approximation.This gives a meaningful interpretation:- \\(\eta\kappa_t<1\\): The step has not yet reached the minimum along the previous descent direction.- \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\): The step approximately reaches that directional minimum.- \\(\eta\kappa_t>1\\): The step has passed that directional minimum, causing the gradient component along the previous direction to reverse.Importantly, reaching the directional minimum does not imply reaching a stationary point of the full multidimensional loss. The remaining gradient can be perpendicular to the previous direction.There is also a special case: if the gradient lies entirely along a Hessian eigenvector, \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\) can make \\(g_t=0\\) in the quadratic model. In that case, the cosine similarity \\(\rho_t\\) is undefined rather than zero.The central insight: \\(\eta\kappa_t=1\\) is a directional critical point where the gradient transitions from positive to negative alignment with its previous value. It represents locally optimal progress along the previous gradient direction, not necessarily an instability threshold or a full optimum.

comments.highlighted_text: The ratio in Eq. (19) is an approximation to an expectation of normalized inner products, rather than an exact identity. For independent, identically distributed nonzero gradients at fixed parameters, the exact expected cosine is nonnegative: it equals the squared norm of the mean unit gradient. Thus this comparison describes the attenuation of common di- rectional alignment toward zero; it cannot describe negative expected alignment caused by parameter motion. Along an SGD trajectory, curvature couples successive updates and can induce negative alignment even when sampling noise is large. Equation (19) therefore does not predict how a destructive regime responds to batch size. That response also depends on the evolving full gradient and its interaction with the sampled updates.

Gradient misalignment: \\(\rho_t<0\\). Consecutive gradients must point in sufficiently opposing directions.2. Gradient norm growth: \\(\\|g_t\\|>\\|g\_{t-1}\\|\\). The current gradient must have a larger norm than the previous one.Both are necessary, but neither is sufficient individually. The negative alignment must be strong enough to satisfy the boxed inequality.Key insight: In the large-batch limit of this approximation, loss spikes require the combination of gradient norm growth and sufficiently strong negative gradient alignment. Simply having a large gradient norm is not enough.
